doc.title: Dick Spottswood interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, February 13, 2023

title: Earliest music memory: the Ink Spots and Jimmy Blythe's lick
summary: At age four he heard the Ink Spots and later recognized their opener in a Ma Rainey record with Jimmy Blythe; Rowe calls it a community lick.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Growing up with radio, records and family listening

blocks.x: It’s funny how things turn out like that. I’m going to — this is a tough question perhaps — can you remember the first recorded music that you heard that sort of struck a nerve with you, that made your ears perk up?

I can’t remember not liking music at all or not responding to it. I guess sort of an answer to your question is what are my earliest music memories and there’s one that really sticks out. I was born in 1937 so I would have been four I think when I heard the Ink Spots I guess it was, singing “I Don’t Want to Set the World on Fire.” I didn’t respond to the Ink Spots so much as to the idea of arson, and the whole planet going up and at age four when people say things like that you hear them literally. So I remember asking my mom, “Why does that man want to blow up the world?” or words to that effect. And then I remember that recording again many, many, many years later when I was listening to Ma Rainey singing “Don’t Fish in my Sea” and if you’ll recall the Jimmy Blythe opener to that song where he goes [scats]. I’m thinking I’ve heard that somewhere before. And sure enough I went back like, this is only recently too, so I went back and dialed up the Ink © Fillius Jazz Archive -2-

Spots’ record and there was Jimmy Blythe’s little opener. So they ripped that off from him, right? Or at least it was around in community folklore section, it was available to the Ink Spots fifteen years after Ma Rainey and Jimmy Blythe picked it up. I thought that was nice. And so I was listening to music carefully when I was only four years old.
That’s terrific. I like that community folklore like for licks. That’s a community lick.
Yeah, yeah, precisely. That’s a much better word.
